source.title: Grokking at the Edge of Linear Separability
source.authors: A. Beck; N. Levi; Yohai Bar-Sinai

record.tranche_reason: The study tests grokking-like delayed generalization using a different, analytically tractable linear logistic-classification setup rather than the original small algorithmic tasks.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own grokking results in synthetic binary classification and varies data separability, noise scale, label fraction, initialization, and optimizer. It does not test the cited Fourier-circuit or mechanistic-progress findings. References to results from other studies are not included as rows.
record.test_reason: The study reports its own training runs of logistic regression on synthetic Gaussian data. Delayed generalization and non-monotonic test loss appear under plain gradient descent near λ=d/N=1/2. This bears on V3 (delay on non-algorithmic data, and what controls it) and V7 (whether the delay needs adaptive optimizers or numerical artifacts). It is a new setting rather than a different method on the original task, so T3 fits better than T2.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that grokking (delayed generalization with non-monotonic test loss) arises in linear logistic classification when the training set is nearly separable from the origin (λ≈1/2) and perpendicular noise is strong. They attribute it to critical slowing down near a point where the overfitting and generalizing solutions exchange stability. They argue the GD-vs-chance-plateau difference is superficial (it depends on optimizer and hyperparameters), and that regularization and numerical precision are not needed. They conjecture that grokking generally occurs near critical or interpolation points, without claiming separability is always the mechanism.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses synthetic Gaussian binary classification and linear logistic regression, with gradient descent and some Adam experiments; it does not reproduce the original modular-arithmetic transformer training recipe.
record.method_sensitivity: The observed dynamics depend on proximity to lambda = 1/2, feature/noise scale, label fraction, initialization, and optimizer. Adam can make the chance-level initial-accuracy pattern more apparent; changing initial conditions can affect test-loss non-monotonicity.

fits_no_version.finding: Changing the initial weight norm or initial bias alters the monotonicity of the test loss and accuracy.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Initial conditions modulate the non-monotonic test-loss signature of grokking in linear logistic models.

fits_no_version.finding: Grokking occurs only below a critical sample ratio λ=1/2 (N>2d), with grokking time diverging at the threshold. There is no weight decay in the setup.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Grokking arises near an interpolation/separability critical point via critical slowing down, without any regularization.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning; Proceedings of the 42nd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 267
record.problems: The evidence concerns a specific synthetic linear binary-classification task, not small algorithmic networks or realistic large-model training. The paper notes that its main accuracy behavior under gradient descent rises from the start, unlike the canonical chance-level plateau, and describes that difference as dependent on optimizer and hyperparameters. Numerical results are often presented in figures; no error bars or confidence intervals are stated for the reported grokking curves.
record.rows_left_out: No additional separately stated outcomes bearing on the tested versions were left out. Other figure-only parameter sweeps and cited findings were not recorded as separate rows when the text did not state a distinct outcome.

untested.parts: No small algorithmic datasets. The training-set-size dependence is shown only through λ in the linear model.
No circuit formation, memorizing-component removal or progress measures.
No images, text or molecules. No lazy-to-rich transition. No weight-norm control of grokking. No init-scale switch of the delay.
No weight decay, no circuit-efficiency comparison, no ungrokking.
Learned algorithms are not compared across runs.
Floating-point/softmax limits are not tested directly. The slingshot-type Adam instability is not examined.

missing.what: Grokking time (gap between train and test accuracy crossing 0.9) diverges as λ→1/2 from below; ||S∞|| also diverges.
missing.locator: Fig. 1 right panels; Fig. 3 right; Fig. 9; Eq. 37

missing.what: Grokking persists for non-isotropic power-law Gaussian and mixture-of-Gaussians inputs at λ=0.45.
Significant grokking with Adam at default settings even at σ=1.
Grokking with pure exponential loss is similar to cross-entropy.

record.verdict_notes: The study frames λ as analogous to the training fraction in Power et al., but does not test algorithmic data. Its finding that a data ratio controls grokking sits awkwardly with V3's 'not the data' framing. No error bars are reported. The paper is not one of the original sources.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not train small networks on small algorithmic datasets or test the claim that delay grows as the algorithmic training set shrinks.

It analyzes the linear-classifier parameters and critical slowing, but does not measure gradual formation of a generalizing circuit, removal of memorizing components, or continuous circuit-progress measures.

Tests a simple synthetic linear classification setting, not images, text, or molecules. It varies noise scale and optimizer, but does not establish a lazy-to-rich transition or test weight-norm control as described in the version.
No LLM pretraining or fine-tuning on realistic data.
No weight-decay intervention, efficiency comparison between circuits, critical dataset-size prediction of the stated kind, or ungrokking test.
Does not identify and compare learned algorithms across runs.
Compares gradient descent with Adam and reports grokking-like behavior under both, but does not test adaptive-optimizer instabilities or floating-point/softmax limits directly.

rows.subject: binary logistic regression (linear model)
rows.operation_detail: Gradient descent on the binary classification task
rows.value: The paper reports a delayed rise in test accuracy; grokking is significant only as lambda approaches 1/2 from below.
rows.note: The paper describes the accuracy as rising from the start in its main gradient-descent setup, rather than remaining at chance for a long initial period.
rows.check: For V7 the row shows the delay persisting under GD, i.e. V7's predicted disappearance is absent. Under GD the test accuracy rises from the start rather than sitting at chance. Fig. 1 right also reports grokking time diverging near λ=1/2; that result is not recorded (see missing).

rows.value: Increasing sigma makes grokking more apparent initially, then the effect saturates; increasing sigma further does not increase grokking time.

rows.value: The paper reports grokking with gradient descent and says Adam can make it more pronounced; it argues the optimizer changes the appearance, not the underlying mechanism.
rows.note: This contradicts the proposition that grokking-like behavior disappears when using ordinary gradient descent, but does not rule out the specific numerical-artifact mechanisms named in V7.
rows.check: V7's predicted effect (the delay vanishing without the adaptive optimizer) is absent: grokking occurs under GD and in the gradient-flow analysis. Marked absent rather than observed.

relationships.condition: Synthetic Gaussian linear classification with λ just below 1/2 and large perpendicular noise
relationships.reason: Delayed test-accuracy rise and non-monotonic test loss occur on non-algorithmic synthetic data (r1, r2, r5, r6). Grokking also persists, with imperfect final accuracy, under relaxed variance or labels (r7, r8, r9).
relationships.display_finding: Test accuracy rose after a delay alongside non-monotonic test loss, and grokking persisted with imperfect final accuracy under relaxed variance or label assumptions.

relationships.condition: Dependence on data properties: separability ratio λ and noise scale σ
relationships.reason: Whether grokking occurs is set by data separability (λ vs 1/2) and data noise scale, not only by the training regime. It is absent above λ=1/2 (r3, r4) and weak at small σ under GD (r10).
relationships.display_finding: Grokking was absent above separability ratio λ=1/2 and weak at small noise scale σ under gradient descent.
